value.overview: The Acorn Woodpecker is a social, medium-sized woodpecker recognized by its red crown, pale forehead and throat, black body, and boldly patterned face. It lives mainly in oak and mixed mountain woodlands, where family groups cooperate in breeding, defense, and food storage. Its unusual habit of placing acorns in thousands of holes drilled into trees, poles, or other wooden structures gives the species its name and helps groups survive periods when food is scarce.
value.classification: The Acorn Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Melanerpes. The Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Melanerpes formicivorus striatipectus.
value.identification: This woodpecker is about 20–23 cm long and has a glossy black back, wings, and upper breast, with white patches on the rump and wings visible in flight. The face is distinctive, combining a red crown, pale yellowish or whitish forehead and throat, and dark cheek markings. The underparts are pale to buff with dark streaking. Males usually show more red on the crown, while females have a narrower red area separated from the forehead by darker feathers. Its loud, nasal “waka-waka” calls are also characteristic.
value.rangeHabitat: The Acorn Woodpecker ranges from the western United States through Mexico and Central America to western Panama, with a separate population in Colombia. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in cool, elevated mountain regions, especially oak-dominated highlands such as the Cordillera de Talamanca and areas around San Gerardo de Dota. It uses mature montane oak forests, mixed oak-conifer woodland, forest edges, and semi-open landscapes with large scattered trees. Important habitat features include acorn-producing oaks, cavities, snags, and suitable surfaces for communal granaries.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur when acorn crops are poor or when groups search for adequate food-storage sites.
value.breeding: Acorn Woodpeckers breed cooperatively in family groups that may include several breeding adults and helpers. More than one female may lay in the same nest cavity, and group members help excavate or maintain the cavity, incubate eggs, feed nestlings, and defend the territory. Nesting usually takes place in a cavity excavated in a tree, often an oak or other mature woodland tree. Several adults share parental duties, and young birds may remain with the group and assist in later breeding attempts.
value.dietFeeding: Acorns are a major food resource, especially in oak woodlands, and are stored in holes that groups maintain as communal granaries. The birds also eat insects and other arthropods, which they obtain by probing bark, gleaning foliage, and searching crevices. Fruit, seeds, sap, and occasionally small vertebrate food items may supplement the diet. In Costa Rica, their feeding is closely associated with montane oaks and other trees that provide both food and storage sites.
value.behavior: This is one of the most social woodpeckers. Groups maintain year-round territories and communicate with loud calls, rattles, and active displays. Members cooperate in guarding granaries, defending nest cavities, raising young, and repairing storage holes. Birds often forage conspicuously on trunks and branches, moving rapidly between trees. They may use utility poles, fence posts, and buildings as substitute storage surfaces where natural granary trees are scarce. Their communal behavior makes them noisy and readily noticeable in suitable habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing overall, although local populations may fluctuate with acorn production and habitat conditions.
